report.source_text: CT-guided drainage was performed by interventional radiology, 15 cc of purulent material was removed and a 12 French pigtail catheter was placed. The abscess grew Group B streptococcus (GBS). Pathology revealed bacteria, no evidence of fungal growth, and no evidence of malignant cells. The acid-fast bacillus (AFB) smear was negative for mycobacteria.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 61-year-old male presented with acute abdominal pain, hematemesis, right shoulder pain, and right anterior chest fullness. Initial chest X-ray was unremarkable. A subsequent CT scan of the chest revealed a 6.5x3.8cm complex right pleural space collection with air foci within the right pectoral muscles. CT-guided drainage yielded purulent material, which on microbiology grew Group B Streptococcus (GBS). Pathology confirmed bacteria, with no evidence of fungal growth, malignant cells, or acid-fast bacilli. The patient was initially treated with Piperacillin-Tazobactam, then switched to Ampicillin/Sulbactam based on sensitivities. Despite an initial plan for surgical intervention, the patient self-removed the drain and declined surgery. Following multidisciplinary discussion, the infection resolved, as evidenced by a chest radiograph six months later.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: CT chest revealed a complex right pleural space collection with air foci within the right pectoral muscles, indicative of empyema necessitans.
Microbiology of the purulent material grew Group B Streptococcus (GBS).
Pathology of the drained material showed bacteria, no fungal growth, no malignant cells, and negative AFB smear.
Antibiotic treatment was initiated with Piperacillin-Tazobactam and switched to Ampicillin/Sulbactam based on sensitivities.
The patient declined surgical intervention and self-removed the drain.
Chest radiograph six months later showed resolution of the infection.
